objective: Circle and Triangle Side-by-Side. Now see the magic connection: the circle on the left and its unwrapped triangle on the right. As you highlight different rings, watch the corresponding strip light up in the triangle. Each ring becomes a horizontal strip — the connection between circle and triangle is direct and visible

finalists.title: Construction History Stepper Through Ring Additions
finalists.narrative_wrapper: The student sees an empty workspace with two empty frames labeled 'Circle' and 'Triangle'. Step-by-step controls let them walk through a construction process: each step forward adds one new ring to the circle and simultaneously adds the corresponding strip to the triangle. They can step backward to remove rings and strips in reverse order, seeing the shapes build up or break down one layer at a time.
finalists.manipulated_variable: The construction step number (discrete integer count), which determines how many ring-strip pairs have been added to the respective shapes
finalists.primary_visual_feedback: Each forward step causes a single new ring to grow from the center outward in the circle frame while simultaneously a new horizontal strip appears and settles into position in the triangle frame, both with matching color coding. Stepping backward removes the most recently added pair with a gentle dissolve. A numeric counter shows 'Step X of N rings'.
finalists.goal_structure: Free exploration through the discrete construction sequence, with students encouraged to observe what happens at specific step counts (e.g., step 1, step 5, final step) and compare early versus late stages
finalists.causal_chain_exposed: The numeric step counter, the current ring radius value displayed for the active step, the corresponding strip length shown as the circumference formula 2πr for that radius, the accumulating area count in both shapes updated after each step, and color-coded matching between each ring-strip pair added
finalists.trace_strategy: All previously added rings and strips remain fully visible and maintain their color coding throughout the stepping process, creating a complete construction history that shows the accumulated structure at each moment, rather than hiding earlier steps
finalists.aha_moment: By stepping forward and watching the area accumulate, students realize that adding rings from inside-out (or outside-in) creates a systematic pattern where each strip's length grows proportionally to its radius, and the stacking creates the slanted edge of the triangle—the formula πr² emerges from summing all these strips, which is exactly the triangle's area ½ × base × height
finalists.feasibility_sketch: The design requires standard web UI parts like stepper controls, color-coded SVG/canvas shapes, and live readouts.
finalists.weakness: The design may rely heavily on color coding, which could be a challenge for colorblind users.

finalists.title: Hover to Highlight Corresponding Ring and Strip
finalists.narrative_wrapper: You see a circle divided into rings on the left and a triangle on the right. As you move your mouse over each ring in the circle, that ring lights up and simultaneously the matching horizontal strip in the triangle lights up. You can sweep across all the rings to see how each one maps to its triangle strip.
finalists.manipulated_variable: Mouse position hovering over concentric rings in the circle, selecting which ring index is active
finalists.primary_visual_feedback: The hovered ring in the circle highlights with color/glow, and simultaneously the corresponding horizontal strip in the triangle highlights with matching color, both appearing immediately under and adjacent to the cursor path
finalists.goal_structure: Free exploration with implicit encouragement to hover over all rings from center to edge to see the complete correspondence
finalists.causal_chain_exposed: The radius of each ring, the circumference of each ring (visible as the length of the corresponding triangle strip), and the vertical position in the triangle (matching the radial position in the circle)
finalists.trace_strategy: None - the concept focuses on spatial correspondence rather than temporal sequence, and keeping only one ring-strip pair highlighted at a time maintains clarity of the one-to-one mapping
finalists.aha_moment: The outer rings of the circle become the longer strips at the base of the triangle, revealing that the triangle's slanted edge represents how circumference grows with radius
finalists.feasibility_sketch: The core primitives needed are SVG/canvas for drawing and highlighting shapes, with no significant runtime risk.
finalists.weakness: The design may not explicitly guide learners to understand the mathematical implications of the visual correspondence without additional context or explanation.

narrative_draft.text:
You've seen individual rings unwrap into strips. You've seen the triangle emerge from those strips. But how does a circle *become* a triangle, layer by layer, before your eyes?

Start with an empty workspace: two frames, one waiting for a circle, one waiting for a triangle. Step forward once, and the first ring appears at the center of the circle—simultaneously, the first strip settles into place at the base of the triangle, glowing with the same color. Step forward again. A new ring wraps around the first, slightly longer, and a matching strip stacks on top in the triangle, a bit wider than the one below. Each step forward adds one more ring-strip pair, and you can watch the circle grow outward while the triangle climbs upward, both shapes building together in perfect sync. Step backward anytime to peel away the layers in reverse, ring by ring, until you're back to the empty frames.

As you step through the construction, notice the pattern: each ring's radius determines its strip's length, so the strips grow steadily longer as you move outward from the center. That's why the triangle's edge isn't vertical—it slants upward in a straight line, height rising in lockstep with the growing radius. When you reach the final ring at radius *r*, you've built a complete circle of area πr² and a complete triangle with base 2πr (the circumference) and height *r*. The triangle's area formula, ½ × base × height, gives you ½ × 2πr × r = πr². The circle and triangle aren't just related—they're the same area, constructed from identical pieces, one step at a time.
